utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, yesterday we reached page 72 of your expert report. On that page, in discussing the change of the mission in Croatia, you point to the order by General Kadijevic and on this page, on page 72, you say, the changes that General Kadijevic discusses, which start from March 1991, meant a radical change of two constitutional tasks of the armed forces against an external and internal aggression. Is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on page 72, in my report, I don't point to a specific order by General Kadijevic. I only mention what General Kadijevic says in his book when he talks about the evolution of the mission of the JNA starting mid-March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the SFRY armed forces under the constitution of the SFRY, Article 240, that's on page 4 of your expert report, have the obligation to defend the country from the internal aggression which in fact the Croat and Slovene illegal formations, secessionist formations, constituted?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the mission of the SFRY armed forces, as I mention it in my report covered four things, and I referred for that to Article 92 of the 1982 all people's Defence law. According to that Article 82, the SFRY armed forces were to safeguard or to protect the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and social order of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If the armed forces had the constitutional obligation to safeguard the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia, did this mean that the SFRY armed forces had the constitutional obligation to prevent the secession of Croatia and Slovenia by armed force?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is more like a legal question because the SFRY armed forces received their orders from the Supreme Command. Supreme Command consisting of the Presidency, so a body which represents all the six republics of the SFRY including the two autonomous regions, and I would -- my answer would be that again, the constitutional mission is one thing. We see that due to the developments within the SFRY, not only in Slovenia and Croatia but also in other republics of the SFRY and most importantly in Serbia in 1991, that there -- well, I would assume that the Supreme Command would take the necessary measures in order to implement the mission and if they want to adjust the mission, to adjust the mission of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given that you cited the SFRY constitution provision which points to the obligation of the armed forces to safeguard the territorial integrity and inviolability of the territory of Yugoslavia, my question to you is: Do the SFRY armed forces have the constitutional obligation to prevent any part of Yugoslav territory from seceding, by force?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I answered that question in my reply to the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you want the witness to give you an interpretation of the constitutional obligations as they are stated in the constitution of this country or of the SFRY, or do you expect this witness to give you expert opinion on what happened in the region based on the constitution that was prevalent at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the second question was put to the witness precisely in order for the expert to answer the question from the perspective of what the SFRY constitution stipulated and what obligations were in place for safeguarding the territorial integrity of the country and that was the gist of my question and rather than what was going on on the ground at the time. My question was, was the -- in principle, was the obligation of the armed forces to protect the integrity of the country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that question a question appropriate for the people who drafted the constitution, what they intended? He can only tell us what it provides. He can't tell us what it was intended to mean, can he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Respectfully, Your Honours, I asked the witness this question because he cited these provisions of the constitution and he spoke of their violations. So my question was not what was happening before or after that but, rather, what these provisions provided, in terms of the protection of territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then, Mr. Milovancevic. You may carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, on page 73 of your report, you identify by quoting Mr. Kadijevic's book, two phases of the armed conflict in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, the two phases I have discussed in my report between the pages 73 and 76 are based on the two phases General Kadijevic identifies in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you indicate in your report that according to Mr. Kadijevic's book, the first phase of the conflict in Croatia was characteristic in terms of it starting with an attack against the Serbs in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. Mr. Kadijevic identifies the start of the first phase of the conflict by what he describes as the first attacks on Serbs in the Serbian Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what General Kadijevic states in his book, which you have been quoting quite a lot, about Croatia's preparations for a war and about the implementation of this phase?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is correct that I read the book by General Kadijevic but I don't recall exactly what General Kadijevic stated about what Mr. Milovancevic called Croatian preparations for a war. As I mentioned in the beginning of my testimony, this report focuses on the TO of the SAO Krajina and then RSK, and also the SVK and the relations between these organisations and Milan Martic. Analysing or studying Croatian or what is called Croatian war preparations or the establishment of armed forces in Croatia was not part of -- is not part of the subject of my report, and therefore I didn't mention it in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I was not the one discussing Croatia's preparations but in view of the fact that you quoted Mr. Kadijevic's book and related what he said about the first and the second phases and about what was going on on the ground in Croatia and in view of the fact that his book does relate something about these preparations, I asked you whether you were familiar with this. You told me you were not, because you had told me you were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see on the screen Exhibit 24, that's General Kadijevic's book, on page 67 in the English version, or rather page 125 in the B/C/S. I apologise, page 68 in the English version. The title is, "The war in Croatia." Or it may even be page 67.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, could you please on page 67 below the heading, "War in Croatia," read the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The war in Croatia. After the Supreme Command meeting held from March the 12th to the 15th 1991, when the SFRY Presidency rejected the proposal of the Supreme Command's General Staff to impose a state of emergency in the country and have the JNA disarm and disband paramilitary formations in Yugoslavia, Croatia accelerated its political and military preparations to secede from Yugoslavia and placed the Serb nation in Croatia in a state of total unconditional subjugation. In the attempts to achieve this the Croatian authorities resorted to all the Ustasha methods known from the days of the fascist independent state of Croatia. Apart from the protection of the Serb nation received" -- excuse me. "Apart from the protection the Serb nation received from the JNA, Serbs in Croatia were compelled to organise themselves in defence of their homes, their lives, and their national identity."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Given that you refer to General Kadijevic's statement about the first phase of the armed conflict in Croatia, which lasted from July through to September 1991, do you recall what General Kadijevic said about the objective that Croatia had in the first phase of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- General Kadijevic's interpretation of the Croatian objectives are included in the paragraph I just read out on page 67, but I would make -- like to make a general comment about how I used the book of Kadijevic because I think there is a misunderstanding about the analytical process. In the analytical process it's very -- you try to avoid to use only one source to describe the attitude or the activities of your opponent. Now, as I mentioned yesterday, I used General Kadijevic's book as one of several sources to explain the evolution of the goals of the JNA during the time period that started more or less at the latest, I mean, in summer 1991. I did include General Kadijevic's book from 1993 but I also included orders and statements General Kadijevic made when he was still the federal secretary of people's defence. I also included statements, official statements by General Adzic who was the chief of General Staff at the time in 1991, as well as more specific orders from JNA units. If I were to discuss or analyse the Croatian objectives in the conflict, I may use the book by Kadijevic but I would also use -- try to find other sources and more specifically official documents from the Croatian forces as I did when I discussed the goals of the JNA. I think that is an essential principle of the work of analysis and that's something I wanted to highlight now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, under section 3, you quoted General Kadijevic repeatedly, drawing upon his book, and you quoted several sentences from his book, which have their own context. You have taken them out of the spatial and temporal context and you have taken them out of the contents of the entire book, and used them to arrive at conclusions that were completely different to what General Kadijevic was trying to show. I simply wanted to establish whether you have properly quoted parts of his book. That's why I'd like you to read one passage from his book on page 68, that's in the English version, and that's page 126 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that the comment Mr. Milovancevic just made is an incorrect representation of my report. Because when you look at the report, under the heading 3, evolution of the mission of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia, there are several subheadings. It goes from A to F. In subheading A, indeed, I discuss Kadijevic's book. However, on page 76, there is a subheading B, which mentions the declaration on the 1st of October by the reduced SFRY Presidency of a state of imminent threat of war. Next I mention under the same heading I mention as I discussed earlier today the statement General Kadijevic had published on the 3rd of October 1991 in the issue number 35 of the bulletin of the information service of the SSNO. When we continue in the subheading C I mention the confidential letter number 6-83 that was issued by the SFRY armed forces morale administration and which is attributed to General Adzic. In the subheading D, I discuss a strictly confidential order number 2256-1 by General Kadijevic which dates from the 10th of December 1991 and which specifically mentions the protection of the Serb population. In the subparagraph E on page 83 of the English version, I quote from the report on the combat readiness of the 2nd military district where the 9th Corps provides its view of the -- how it accomplished the missions of the SFRY armed forces. So I don't think that I misquoted General Kadijevic somewhere or that I took his comments out of context because the comments I used I took from -- or the paragraphs I took from Mr. Kadijevic's book correspond with orders and statements he made at the time of the events in 1991 as well as orders and statements of General Adzic and subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm not trying to interpret your report in an incorrect way. I'm just trying to verify two issues. One is how you're quoting Mr. Kadijevic. We are just checking this to see whether you quote his words accurately or whether perhaps some of his thoughts are taken out of context. The Defence does not believe that what Mr. Kadijevic wrote is the holy Bible, that is not subject to any analysis and inspection. What we are trying to do is establish whether what you quoted was quoted correctly, whether it was -- it reflected accurately the spirit in which it was written, and we are also trying to establish what actually happened on the ground. Therefore I would like to kindly ask you not to evade answering my question. I would like to ask you to do the same thing you did when answering the questions of the OTP. So would you now please read passage 2 of General Kadijevic's text on page 68 concerning the two phases of the war, what happened in phase one in Croatia and what actually happened on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Would you please read the third paragraph from the top? It starts with the words, "In this phase, Croatia's aim."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In this first phase Croatia's aim was to use the police and army to establish control over Serb regions in Croatia and break down any Serb resistance. This was seen as a necessary stage in achieving the general goal of a sovereign Croatian state which apart from all the territory lying within the administrative borders of the existing Republic of Croatia would in the later stage of Yugoslavia's dismemberment also encompass other territories with a majority Croatian population, i.e. territories to which for one reason or another the leadership of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, aspired."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. As you have mentioned the words of Mr. Kadijevic to the effect that the conflict in Croatia unfolded in two phases and we are now discussing the first phase, can you tell us what Mr. Kadijevic's thoughts are in the book about the strategy and tactics of Croatia in implementing this first phase?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting. I was expecting a question whether about whether there was out of context because we heard a couple of speeches from the Defence saying that he was worried about Mr. Theunens taking passages out of context. It seems to me the procedure would be to point him at passages and then ask him questions about that. What's happening instead is that he asked Mr. Theunens to read out a passage and then no question follows and it appears we are moving on to a new subject. I would ask that the counsel put questions to the witness rather than simply read passages to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have an answer to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The aim of this type of examination is to finally reach an answer to the thesis presented by the expert witness, namely whether, in the first and the second phase of the conflict in Croatia, any changes occurred in the constitutional role of the JNA and whether this was in conformity with the constitution, in order to reach an answer to this major question, the witness first needs to answer some minor questions. Perhaps this is not in the order that is clearly visible or clearly obvious but I'm first asking the witness whether he knows something about the tactics and the strategy, in order for us to be able to assess the goals of both sides. The expert witness spoke only about the goals of one side, and we need to see what an eyewitness to the events, namely General Kadijevic, thinks about the events. Based on the quotations of General Kadijevic in the expert report, one can gain a completely different impression than what Mr. Kadijevic actually intended with his book. That's what I'm trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you know, the whole morning and perhaps even yesterday, you have been engaging in argument with the witness. Your questions are very argumentative. And I was counting the lines on a previous page now of your question to this witness. Your question goes beyond 15 lines. You have made an allegation against this witness that he's quoting the book out of context, and in the light of that allegation, you made the witness read a passage from the book. And we are all waiting to see you point out how he quoted Kadijevic out of context. Now, point that out. Don't leave it and go to the next point and then say that the aim is to see how Kadijevic's views were on the other side of that -- the struggle. You got to tell us how this witness, before you go to how Kadijevic views the struggle, tell us how this witness quotes the author out of context. And do so by putting questions to him, not by giving speeches to him and then expecting him to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Theunens, bearing in mind the two paragraphs that you have read out, was the conduct of federal armed forces on the ground in specific circumstances a reaction to the conduct of the opposing side, namely the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to repeat the goal of the aim of my report. My report aims -- studies, my report studies the SAO Krajina and then the RSK TO and SVK and relations between these organisations and Milan Martic. Whether or not the activities of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia were a reaction on activities from the Croatian forces is something I did not investigate, so it's impossible for me to answer that question. I don't think it would be correct from an analytical point of view to just use one source, i.e. the book of Kadijevic, in order to assess the intentions of the Croatian forces and/or the way how whether the JNA acted or reacted in certain circumstances, whether the initiative came from the Croats or from the JNA and local Serbs. That was not the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Theunens. You wrote, and also gave evidence here in the courtroom, about not having studied the Croatian forces. However, you used General Kadijevic's book, and when General Kadijevic writes that at one point in time the armed forces protected the Serb population, you interpret that as a change of the constitutional role of the armed forces. This is why I'm asking you now, and I ask kindly, that you answer me to the extent you are able to as a military officer, namely, in the first phase, and you refer to General Kadijevic's words about Croatian forces attacking the Serb population, under those circumstances, was it possible for the JNA not to protect the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to page 12 of the English version of my report, where I quoted when I was discussing the mission of the SFRY armed forces, I first mentioned the article 92 of the 1982 all people's Defence law and then I also quoted from a 1983 manual from the federal Secretariat for People's Defence, a manual called strategy of armed conflict. And in that manual, in chapter 4, it is mentioned, and I will read from my report, "SFRY armed forces together with other forces of all people's Defence and social self-protection, protect the interests of all nations and nationalities and all working people and citizens of the socialist, self-managing, and non-aligned Yugoslavia and are the expression of their readiness and determination to successfully defend themselves against any aggression."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you quoted the legislative provision, specifically stating that the obligation of the armed forces is to protect all of the population, do you believe, as a military expert, that the JNA and the armed forces had no obligation to protect the Serb population which was at risk during this first phase?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the text I quoted from this 1983 military manual, the JNA as well as the other components of the SFRY armed forces had to protect all nations and nationalities. Now, Mr. Milovancevic claims that the Serb population was at risk. We see in Kadijevic's book that he mentions indeed that the Serb population is at risk but I think if you would have put Mr. Spegelj's book here he would have said that the Croatian population was at risk. So again, I keep on repeating myself but I think it is dangerous to use one single source to try to draw conclusions on the activities or the behaviour of the other side or the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since right now we are not discussing the threat to the Croatian population, and you in your expert report mention Kadijevic's words about the Serb population being fiercely attacked during the first phase, my question was whether the tactics of the Croatian armed forces mentioned by Mr. Kadijevic in his book, namely to group armed formations in Krajina, to spread fear by constantly issuing threats, mostly directed at the Knin Krajina, to occasionally attack appropriately selected populated settlements and to use these tactics in order to break down the Serb morale and prepare an all-out attack against Serbian Krajina in its entirety or partially; bearing this in mind, bearing in mind the situation that existed at the time, in your view was it appropriate, in view of the constitutional role of the armed forces of the federation to protect the Serb population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you really hope to get an answer to this question? You've been asking this question in different forms for the last 15 minutes. The witness has given you what he says is his answer. What do you want -- do you want to beat him into saying what you want him to say? You don't want to accept what he's telling you? Because now you're asking the same question over and over again, in different forms, and we are not making progress. If you think that this witness is not answering your questions, it's for you to argue at the end of the case that the witness did not answer your questions and -- but to try and browbeat him now is not going to make progress. It's not going to give you the answer you want. He's giving you the answers as he understands them and that's how he's answering you. He's been telling you that he can't use one source to analyse. He's got to use several sources. He's given you this answer many times. What do you expect from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for this caution. I'm expecting the witness to give an answer to the following question: Is defending the civilian population something that is in conformity with the constitutional role of the armed forces? This witness quotes General Kadijevic and General Kadijevic says that it was the constitutional role of the armed forces, and then the witness draws a conclusion that this reflected a radical change of the constitutional role of the armed forces. I will not, however, insist any longer on this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, I think we move from protecting the Serb population to defending the civilian population, and again it is not me who states or who concludes that there is a radical change. The word "radical" is a direct quotation from the book of Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed that's what I wanted to say to Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much, Mr. Theunens. Mr. Milovancevic, if you look at page 72, where -- of the report, you will see under paragraph 2, paragraph 2 under the heading evolution of the mission of the JNA during the conflict in Croatia, that he -- the witness there says, this implied, according to Kadijevic, that the two constitutionally defined tasks of the SFRY armed forces, including the JNA, defence against an external and internal aggression, were, "radically" changed into. He's quoting. It's not his conclusion. It's not this witness's conclusion. This witness is quoting. So please, as you attack him for quoting the book out of context, don't misquote him, too. You were asking him the question -- you were asking him the question is defending the civilian population something that is in conformity with the constitutional role of the armed forces. Mr. Theunens, will you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As such, Your Honour, indeed that was part of the constitutional mission of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what part it was. The question is, is defending a civilian population in conformity with the constitutional obligation? Your answer should be yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may ask the next question, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On page 74 of your report, you say that in the second phase of the armed conflict in Croatia, the JNA had two tasks. Prior to that, on page 73, you say that the second phase began in late summer of 1991 with the attacks of the Croats against military units and garrisons in Croatia, and that this phase continued until the Vance Plan was accepted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's General Kadijevic who identifies these phases in his book and who defines the events that mark the start and the end of the different phase. It's not me who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: While preparing your expert report, did you come across some information indicating that such armed attacks against the JNA units and garrison in Croatia from September of 1991 until the implementation of the Vance Plan existed?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I've come across information from various sources, open sources, JNA situation reports and even witness statements, if I recall well, that indicate that from September 1991 onwards, a number of JNA barracks and garrisons in Croatia were blocked and in some cases even the term "besieged" was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about the Brioni memorandum from July of 1991, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I heard of the Brioni memorandum or Brioni agreement of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the Brioni memorandum represent an agreement drafted with the facilitation provided by the European Community, and was it aimed to delay or postpone the secession of Slovenia and Croatia by three months?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that the postponement of the declaration of independence was one of the points of the Brioni agreement but I don't know whether that was a, or the, specific goal, nor am I familiar with the other goals or points of the Brioni agreement, and I should add the postponement of the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia to complete my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen that document at all, the Brioni agreement, mandating this moratorium?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've seen the Brioni agreement prior to coming to the ICTY, but I don't recall seeing it during my professional activities at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that you have seen the agreement and you know in general terms that it provided for the postponement of the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia by three months, does this mean that the second phase of the armed conflict in Croatia began during this three-months' moratorium, since second phase, as you say, started in September?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you refer us to where the witness mentioned three months, Mr. Milovancevic, on the text, on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not saying that the witness mentioned it. It is simply a general provision contained in the Brioni memorandum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your question is -- since you said that you have seen the -- your question is, since you say that you have seen the agreement and you know in general terms that it provided for the postponement of the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia by three months; this is what you say he says. You are attributing words to him that he has never mentioned now you're saying you didn't attribute those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question contained two sentences; perhaps based on which one could have gained such an impression. It wasn't my intention to put words in the witness's mouth. Let me clarify, please, in order to ensure that it is clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just put a question, one question, don't make two questions. Put one question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that the Brioni memorandum dated 7th of July 1991 contained a provision about a moratorium which would last for three months?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that the Brioni agreement or memorandum contained a provision for the postponement of the declaration of independence of Slovenia and Croatia but I don't recall exactly how many months this postponement was supposed to last.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago you said that you came across some information which indicated that during the so-called second phase of the armed conflict in Croatia, the Croatian forces launched attacks on the JNA units and garrisons in Croatia. These JNA units and garrisons, were they present in Croatia prior to this happening for many years?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be more correct to say that I did come across information that according to which, from the beginning of September onwards or from end of August, Croats started to block and in some cases even besiege certain barracks and garrisons of the JNA in Croatia. I didn't analyse that aspect in detail because it is outside the framework of my report, so I'm not in a position which force or which units were exactly involved in or which individuals were exactly involved in blocking or even besieging JNA barracks, nor am I in a position to say which barracks were being blocked or besieged and for how long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, were these barracks and garrisons that were blocked part of an infrastructure that was present not only in Croatia, which was one of the federal units of Yugoslavia but in other parts of Yugoslavia as well, for quite a long time?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the few examples I remember, the answer would be affirmative, but again, if -- I cannot give an answer without having studied the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the fact that the units and garrisons that were blocked and under attack mostly located in towns in the Republic of Croatia because that was the way the barracks were spread out in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the examples I recall indeed some of the barracks were located in cities. Now, I wouldn't want to expand that answer for all the JNA barracks and garrisons because I haven't studied that aspect of the conflict in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In many parts of your report, you talk of the constitutional position of the armed forces of the SFRY, including who issued orders on the engagement of this armed force. Wasn't the SFRY Presidency the one that ordered the engagement of units under the SFRY legislation and constitution? And I have the year 1991 in mind.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that according to the SFRY constitution, it was up to the SFRY Presidency as it was the Supreme Command, to issue orders to the SFRY armed forces. However, as I've also attempted to point out in the section of the report we are discussing at the moment, there are indications, and one source for that is the book by Borisav Jovic, last days of the SFRY, that in the course of 1991, some kind of parallel command structure became active which did not include all the members of the SFRY Presidency. And this is for example mentioned on page 69, subparagraph 3, where I refer to the published diary of Borisav Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: According to the strict provisions of the SFRY constitution and the law on the armed forces, could anyone apart from the SFRY Presidency order the engagement of the SFRY armed forces and their involvement in combat?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I've answered that question in the previous -- my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this answer of yours mean that under the constitution there wasn't any other body apart from the SFRY Presidency that could order the engagement the SFRY armed forces? And please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who ordered the blockade of the JNA garrisons and the launching of attacks on the JNA units and garrisons in Croatia which lasted from August through to the implementation of the Vance Plan in 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I will again repeat myself but the few examples I do recall, there I think it was a combination of maybe local authorities on the Croatian level who ordered such a blockade, as well as spontaneous movements of certain people in Croatia who believed that it was useful to blockade certain JNA barracks or garrisons. Now, this is obviously not authoritative answer because I have not studied the block or the blockade of JNA barracks and garrisons in Croatia in detail so I don't know which command structures, if any, were behind these blockades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the local authorities or the population themselves decided to block the JNA units and garrisons and attack them. Would not this, in your terminology, in military terminology, mean that an armed rebellion occurred?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was incomplete in my previous answer because I seem to recall now that there were media statements at the time by President Tudjman, the president of Croatia, where he called or announced blockades of barracks, and I think that was in September 1991. Now, to answer your question, blockades can also be carried out by peaceful means so it doesn't have to be an armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since the blockade, whatever its character was, turned into armed attacks that lasted until the Vance Plan came into force, were these armed attacks, in fact, an armed rebellion or not, in military terminology?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure whether the blockades lasted until the coming into effect or the coming into force of the Vance Plan. The Vance Plan was agreed upon on the second of January but its implementation started later and was a gradual process. And because I didn't study the blockades as such, I cannot draw a conclusion on whether it was an armed rebellion or whether it was rebellion or whether it was something else. And I apologise but I add that it was the 2nd of January 1992 for the signing of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the Geneva agreement which was signed on the 23rd November 1991, by -- which was facilitated by a special envoy of the United Nations, Mr. Vance, and the then-president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Tudjman, then the president of Serbia, Milosevic, and General Kadijevic, the chief of the General Staff of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time, General Kadijevic was the federal Secretary for People's Defence and because a state of imminent threat of war had been declared, Kadijevic also carried out the duties of the Chief of Staff of the staff of the Supreme Command. I did mention the November -- 23rd of November 1991 cease-fire agreement in my report without, however, going into details as to the various aspects of the cease-fire agreement..

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If the special envoy of the UN General secretary Mr. Vance interceded on behalf of the UN for a cessation of the conflict on the ground, did this thus -- did it not mean that there were armed conflicts on the ground at the time and not just merely blockades?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, but, and that's also visible through the report. In addition, I mean blockades were only one aspect of the conflict. The operations that took place in areas that were considered Serb, and I'm quoting now actually Mr. Kadijevic, he mentions the Serbian regions in Croatia. There were in many areas combat operations between local Serbs according to documents I have seen often supported by JNA or at least JNA and local Serb TO working together under single command as well as Croatian forces on the other side, or even operations led by JNA, including also local Serb TO and SAO Krajina MUP, in order to establish Serbian control over certain areas considered Serbian, Kijevo being one of the examples. So the blockade is only one aspect of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a while ago that President Tudjman had called on the population to block the barracks. Wasn't such conduct by the president of the state an invitation to a rebellion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a political question which is outside the framework of my report and which -- for which I'm unqualified to provide an authoritative answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this may be the appropriate time for a break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will adjourn and come back at quarter to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Theunens, we discussed the president of Croatia, Tudjman's call on the population to mount the blockade of the JNA barracks and units. And that is what we will pursue. You mentioned the Geneva agreement of 23rd November 1991, which was reached with the facilitation of Mr. Vance. I'd like to know whether this agreement was an interlude to the peacekeeping operation of the UN in Yugoslavia, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. The 23rd of November 1991 Geneva cease-fire agreement was considered a prelude or a precursor to the signing of the Vance Plan which regulated the peacekeeping operation in Croatia and -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Vance Plan regulated the peacekeeping operations in Croatia. Doesn't the Vance Plan provide for the peacekeeping operation in Yugoslavia, in fact, that's what it was called, rather than in Croatia only?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honours, that the aim of the Vance Plan was to create the conditions, peace and security, that would allow a peaceful solution to the conflict in Yugoslavia, as it is officially called. Now, if I remember well, when it comes to the implementation of the Vance Plan and the deployment of peacekeeping forces, most of these forces were deployed in Croatia. I mean by this that the UNPAs, the UN-protected areas covered only territory -- that was part of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where the UN forces are deployed is one matter, whereas the title of the peace operation in a country is a different matter. Wasn't the official title of the peace operation the peace operation in Yugoslavia, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I meant -- I replied to the previous question that the aim of the Vance Plan was to create conditions with regard to peace and security, to allow a political solution or to allow negotiations for a political solution for the conflict in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you seem to be evading the answer. You said that the UN peace plan provided for the peace operation in Croatia, whereas my question to you is: Isn't the UN peace plan -- wasn't the UN peace plan put in place to conduct peace operations in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I think just the question above this one, the answer above this question that you've asked says, "Yes, Your Honours, I meant -- I replied to the previous question that the aim of the Vance Plan was to create conditions with regard to peace and security, to allow a political solution or to allow negotiations for a political solution for the conflict in Yugoslavia." How is he evading your question? He's agreed with you that it was Yugoslavia indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, respectfully, the witness always answers my questions with "yes, but," so I'm never really sure whether the yes part or the but part prevails. I merely asked the witness to answer with a yes or no, rather than provide a detailed explanation. That is why I insisted that the witness answer with a yes or no or I don't know, and if he knows the answer, then he should tell us what it is that he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There was no "but" in the answer that he gave, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Respectfully, Your Honour, he provided an explanation in addition to his affirmative answer, which has the overall undertone of a "but". However, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Page 119 of your expert report, and on two occasions during your testimony you stated that the Vance Plan was concluded on the 2nd of January 1992 by Tudjman and Milosevic. Do you know that these persons did not sign any sort of agreement or pact on that day?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I included in the report, Your Honours, reflects the information I saw when compiling this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you refer us to any document which would indicate what you said, that Tudjman and Milosevic signed the Vance Plan on the 2nd of January 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that I didn't include a specific footnote to substantiate the first sentence on page 119, but if I recall well, it comes from the NIOD chronology I've used and other occasions in the report. I don't have the exact 65 ter number but the NIOD, Netherlands Institute for War Documentation -- it should actually be NIOD -- compiled a chronology of the conflict between 1991 and 1995, referring mainly to open and press sources. Now, it may well be that Tudjman and Milosevic didn't sign the agreement but at least one way or the other they agreed to it because otherwise, I don't think that there would be a UN mission in Croatia. Now, if they agreed verbally, that's fine with me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the report of NIOD is incorrect because Ambassador Okun, a witness of the Prosecution in Milosevic trial on transcript page 19650 to 19651 stated that what is usually considered the Vance Plan is actually a document containing four documents, one being the Geneva Convention, signed on the 23rd of December 1991. The second document is a cease-fire agreement reached between Raseta and Susak on the 2nd of February 1992. These two documents established the situation on the ground and end of hostilities. The third document is a concept for peace operations dated the 3rd of December 1991, and it established technical details, it defined technical details about the location of UNPA zones and so on. The fourth document is a resolution of the Security Council of the United Nations, number 743, dated the 21st of February 1992, which created the peace operation. Are you familiar with these documents, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to thank Mr. Milovancevic for this clarification. I'm familiar with a number of these documents, in particular the United Nations Security Council resolution 743. Now, again I leave it to Your Honours whether the difference between what I wrote in my report and what Mr. Milovancevic explained has a significant impact for the -- on the subject of my report. I would also like to draw your attention to the Exhibit number 65 ter number 917, which was the source I consulted or the main source I consulted to describe the Vance Plan, 65 ter number 917 are the international conference on the former Yugoslavia official papers dating from 1997, and you can find them under the English ERN 01145409, 01145415.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I put to you that all documents that exist, and all exhibits that exist, point to the fact that there was no meeting between Milosevic and Tudjman on the 2nd of January 1992, that no kind of agreement, either verbal or written one, was concluded on that date. Additionally, there is no way to tie that date with the Vance Plan, as you did it. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on my information, the Vance Plan was accepted on the 2nd of January. Now, if that information is correct I'm willing to accept that. Still, I want to emphasise that if there had been no agreement from Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic with the Vance Plan, it would have been very hard to establish the UN peacekeeping mission in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness has not answered the issue as to whether or not there was a meeting, for what it's worth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the information in my report on the top of page 119 is that Tudjman and Milosevic signed the plan. Now, maybe they didn't sign at the same time so I don't imply that there was a meeting. And again, if that is not entirely correct, I'm willing to accept the points made by Mr. Milovancevic but I don't think that has an impact on the essence, on actually the subject matter, where what is really -- which is really important for this -- in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The essence that I'm trying to highlight, Mr. Theunens, is that the peace operation of the UN in Yugoslavia, known as the Vance Plan, is not some kind of a document signed by Milosevic and Tudjman. Rather, it's a UN Security Council resolution. Is that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that United Nations Security Council resolution 743 deals with the Vance Plan and there is also a second, or there are at least two other resolutions that deal with the deployment of the peacekeeping forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Given that you have said that the Vance Plan, let us call it that, could not have been accepted had it not been given approval by Milosevic and Tudjman on the 2nd of January 1992, so the 2nd of January 1992. Do you know that the peace operation defined by the resolution 743 of the UN Security Council of the 21st of February 1992, was adopted after the Secretary-General of the UN, in his report dated the 15th of February 1992, gave recommendations for the peace operation to be put in place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, you have lost me. Could you rephrase that question, make it a bit more direct and condense it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my question was whether Mr. Theunens knew that the UN peace operation was not put into place until the recommendation was given by the Secretary-General to implement the operation? And he gave that recommendation on the 15th of February 1992. That was the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have read the report the Secretary-General drafted for the Security Council on the 21st of February 1992, and I do remember that in that report, reference is made to meetings Mr. Marek Goulding, if I'm correct, he was the chief of the department for peacekeeping operations, also known as DPKO at the UN so the meetings Marek Goulding had with Tudjman, Milosevic, Jovic -- I'm not sure whether it was Kadijevic or Adzic, and when I say meetings, I mean separate meetings and that all these political and military leaders expressed their support to the implementation of the Vance Plan and the deployment of a UN peacekeeping force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that precisely in that document that you just remembered, Mr. Theunens, it is clearly stated that the Secretary-General gave the recommendation only after seeing the letters dating the 6th of February 1992 and the 11th of February 1992 in which President Tudjman accepted such a mission, and after Borisav Jovic, president of the committee for the cooperation between Yugoslavia and the UN, informed him on the 11th of February 1992, that the assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina consented to the plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if Mr. Milovancevic is reading from the report, and then I believe him, I don't recall the exact dates but otherwise I mentioned already in my reply to the previous question that there it was an agreement of Tudjman, Milosevic, Jovic, and then also Adzic or Kadijevic, I'm not sure who of the two Marek Goulding saw in his visits to Croatia and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting these questions to you, Mr. Theunens, precisely because you said that Milosevic and Tudjman accepted the Vance Plan. The Secretary-General of the UN in his written report given to the Security Council states that in fact this agreement was accepted by Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Jovic in writing. Are these two different things, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are indeed two different things, Your Honours, but again as we discussed earlier today we spoke about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. That's quite all right. I apologise for interrupting you. The important thing is to establish that these are two different things. I think we understood each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that the witness be given a chance to explain. He was in the middle of explaining when he was interrupted. I think he should be allowed to continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can you finish your answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. What I wanted to add is that even though these are different things, they are intimately related to each other because without the cease-fire agreement of the 23rd of November 1991, which was agreed by Milosevic, Tudjman, and Kadijevic during which Milosevic also gave certain guarantees to Okun that Serbian volunteers and paramilitaries would abide by the agreement, without that cease-fire agreement, there would have been no agreement on the Vance Plan in February, as it is pointed out here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. You said that the UN troops were deployed to certain areas which were defined as zones and sectors. Can you tell us more about these areas and how they were defined in the UN peace operations plan?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, this is discussed on page 119 of the English version of my report. In the Vance Plan, three UNPAs - UNPA stands for United Nations protected area - were defined, which covered four sectors, sector south, sector north, sector west and sector east. UNPAs were areas or were parts of the territory of the Republic of Croatia where according to the UN Secretary-General, special arrangements were required during an interim period in order to ensure a lasting cease-fire or the maintaining of a lasting cease-fire. I've also seen descriptions for the UNPAs or further detailing of these areas where it is mentioned that these are areas where Serbs constitute a majority or a substantial minority prior to the conflict or as a result of the conflict. And where according or as a result of the conflict, armed or as part of the tensions between the people, armed conflicts had erupted in recent past. The document which is visible on 65 ter -- excuse, me on the e-court, 65 ter number 917, also mentions that the special arrangement in these UNPAs would be of an interim nature and would not prejudge the outcome of political negotiations for a comprehensive settlement of the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the Vance Plan explicitly provide that the UN troops ought to be deployed to the areas where the Serb population constitutes a majority or a substantial minority and in which intercommunal tensions have caused a conflict to erupt?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance Plan states that the UN troops are to be deployed in the UNPAs and I've given the definition of the UNPAs. Now, I want to add, and that's not included in the document, that the boundaries of these UNPAs were the result of negotiations between Croats, Serbs and UN because, of course, each party had its own views on the limits of these UNPAs, geographic limits, and these had to be negotiated and that happened between November and February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say that, Mr. Theunens, between November and February 1992, or is it between November 1991 and February 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, November 1991 and February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you refer us to a document, Mr. Theunens, where the UN troops or, based on which the UN troops were deployed to areas where the Serb population constitutes a majority or a substantial minority as a result of an armed conflict, as you have put it? That is not stipulated in the UN plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, once again, Mr. Milovancevic, you introduced a question of substantial majorities. You said -- you asked the question, "Does the Vance Plan explicitly provide that the UN troops ought to be deployed to the areas where the Serb population constitutes a majority or a substantial minority." Now you're attributing that statement to the witness or has he said it at some other stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the provision of the Vance Plan pertains precisely to the areas where the Serbs constituted a majority or a substantial minority. I am now putting to the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. But the witness has been saying that the Vance Plan applied in the UNPAs areas. He didn't say the UNPAs areas were areas that were either -- which either had the majority of Serbs or a substantial minority of Serbs. He just said it was on an agreement between the three gentlemen. Now, you are now saying to him that he said that those areas were areas where the population of Serbs was in the majority or a substantial minority. I'm just asking you if -- is that what the witness said? If it is what you are proposing to him, tell him that's what you're proposing to him. Don't say that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, line 8, page 32, of the transcript contains the witness's answer to my question about where the UN troops were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get line 8, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, line 8 and 9 reflects the answer of the witness to my question, where he states that the UN troops were deployed to areas, and then he goes on to quote the UN plan, namely the words "where the Serbs constituted a majority or a substantial minority" and then he adds something that is not contained in the UN plan, namely that they became that as a result of an armed conflict. This is the bit that cannot be found in the Vance Plan. This is what I'm putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking for page 32, line 8 to be shown, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm recognising you, but before I ask you to speak, I would like to see page 32, line 8, Mr. Milovancevic, please, where you say this is what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is page 32 of the transcript, as far as I can see, line 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah but my screen doesn't show me page 32. I'm asking to be shown page 32, line 8, Mr. Milovancevic. That's all I'm asking, and if the Court officers are able to help us, they can help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If it's helpful, Your Honour, I've been able to get it on my screen I would be happy to read the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you may, please, it might just help us save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it's important to read just exactly what the witness said because it's slightly different from what Mr. Milovancevic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe the sentence at issue is, "I've also seen descriptions for the UNPAs or further detailing of these areas, where it is mentioned that these are areas where Serbs constitute a majority or a substantial minority, prior to the conflict or as a result of the conflict." I believe that's the sentence at issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've also seen what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I've also seen descriptions for the UNPAs, the protected areas, or further detailing of these areas "where it is mentioned that these are areas where Serbs constitute a majority or a substantial minority prior to the conflict or as a result of the conflict."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not the testimony of the witness. That's a quotation that the witness says --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, that's what the witness said. I was quoting the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, you were quoting him. Thank you, Mr. Black. Is that what you were referring to, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I had in mind, Your Honour. Now I'm referring you to paragraph 8 of the UN Security Council resolution defining the protected areas and stating there would be areas in which Serbs constitute [In English] "Majority or substantial minority of the population and where intercommunal tensions have led to armed conflict in the recent past." [Interpretation] Therefore, Your Honour, I asked the witness about the provisions of the Vance Plan. I didn't ask him about what he read in other documents, comments, and so on. This was the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I think that the definition I gave for the UNPAs corresponded with what is mentioned in the resolution. Now the reason why I mentioned -- why I added that areas where Serbs constitute a majority or substantial minority prior to the conflict, the only reason why I did that is that when I compare during the preparation of my report the territory covered by the UNPAs with maps depicting the 1991 census, there were areas covered by the UNPAs, for example, the municipality of Slunj, where there was a Croatian majority prior to the conflict, and if I recall well, I think it was 60 per cent or more than 60 per cent of Croats and something less than 40 per cent of Serbs, and then as a result of the conflict, the Croatian or largest part of the Croatian population of Slunj was removed or left. So that was the only reason why I added in my reply to the question of Mr. Milovancevic the section on "as a result of the conflict." It is correct that as a result of the conflict, that small passage, is not mentioned in the Vance Plan nor the Security Council resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you study the statistics and statistical analysis of the population in Croatia while preparing your expert report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The results of the 1991 census, which I also include in the atlas that was introduced in the beginning of my testimony, is one of the informations I came across while preparing for this report, for this report, but I didn't include any specific data as such in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your report, you mentioned that the SFRY Presidency declared a state of imminent threat of war in the SFRY on the 1st of October 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I was just locating the source. I think it's the Official Gazette of the 18th of October, the SFRY Official Gazette of the 18th of October. And this has the 65 ter number 1245.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your report on pages 76 and 77, you say that in connection with this Presidency decision or, rather, after this Presidency decision, the army General Veljko Kadijevic issued a public statement to the citizens of Yugoslavia on the 3rd of October. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. This is 65 ter number 65, although it is not a statement specifically to the citizens of Yugoslavia. It is a statement also intended for the international public opinion and the international community because it was also published immediately in English in the English version of The Bilten, i.e. The bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When I said that Mr. Kadijevic gave a statement addressing the citizens of Yugoslavia on the 3rd of October 1991, I literally quoted the name, the title of the statement, which was published in the bulletin, Bilten of the SSNO and the first sentence of this statement. Does the first statement read, "Citizens of Yugoslavia, members of the armed forces of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no dispute about that. It's obvious. But all I wanted to add is that the statement, for example, the Office of the Prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecution has only an English version of the statement because we have a number of issues of the bulletin and the bulletin was specifically intended to provide what the SSNO called themselves the truth about the events in the former Yugoslavia and as it is in English I assume that it is intended for the international community and the international media, even though the statement as such, of course, has in the title, "Citizens of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Could you please read the second paragraph of the statement? That's on page 77, the statement of the federal secretary, the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the second I have quoted in my report or the second from the statement? Because I didn't include the entire statement in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I mentioned the second paragraph as you indicated it on page 77. Therefore, October 1991, citizens of Yugoslavia and then there is one paragraph but I meant the following paragraph or, rather, on page 77 that would be the fourth paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the paragraph that starts with, what is in force?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: "We have." It starts with the words, "We have."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is second, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have been left without a state and from what was seen and heard last night about the March sessions of the Supreme Command, you could also have seen once again in an obvious way what kind of Supreme Commander we have. Some members of the SFRY Presidency continuously prevented the making of decisions with a clear goal of breaking up Yugoslavia by hindering and breaking the army. The federal Prime Minister has joined them with his perfidious deceit. Such an attitude of the Supreme Commander and the Prime Minister towards their own army is not known anywhere else in the world."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Does this paragraph show which session of the Presidency Mr. Kadijevic has in mind? He speaks of the March session and he says that the citizens had the opportunity, the previous night, to view this particular Presidency session -- the March session of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, but I would like to add that my paragraph B which starts on the bottom of page 66, the word "following" is only intended as a kind of -- to show the chronology. I didn't imply -- I didn't necessarily imply a causal link between the first of October decision and the 3rd of October statement. Maybe there is a link, maybe not, but I didn't analyse any causal effect between both events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour that was a little confusing the witness mentioned page 66. I wonder if he meant page 76.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will correct. It was the bottom of page 76 where I used the word "following" to make the link between the 1st of October SFRY Presidency decision and then the 3rd of October Kadijevic statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, at this point we are only discussing this paragraph of Kadijevic's statement of the 3rd of October 1991, and my question did not aim to tie up with any other events. Can one see on the basis of this paragraph that General Kadijevic is addressing the citizens of Yugoslavia and that he is referring to the March sessions of the Presidency of Yugoslavia? I believe your answer was an affirmative one.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, but I've tried to explain because the statement is in English it's also addressed for the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. That is beyond dispute. When mentioning the March Presidency session, the Presidency session from March 1991 when some proposals were rejected, does General Kadijevic have in mind the session held on -- between the 12th and the 15th of March, when the Presidency rejected the declaration of a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is this witness supposed to answer that question? How is he supposed to know what is in the mind of Mr. Kadijevic at this stage, if Mr. Kadijevic doesn't give a date in March himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness does not have to answer the question. He can say that he does not know. My question to him was whether he knew or did not know about it, that the statement has certain context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness has been asked whether he knows what Mr. Kadijevic had in mind. How is he here -- how is he supposed to know what Mr. Kadijevic had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Respectfully, Your Honour, in his statement, Mr. Kadijevic is referring to the session of the Presidency at which some members of the Presidency made it impossible to take some decisions that were to prevent the break-up of the country and backed some proposals that were supposed to lead to the dissolution of the country. And he links it to Ante Markovic and that's why I asked the witness whether he knew that this was the particular session of the Presidency, that's to say in March 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, all what you are saying has nothing to do with my remarks. My remarks have to do with your questioning the witness whether he knows what Mr. Kadijevic had in mind when he made certain statements. I'm saying, how is this witness supposed to know what is in the mind of anybody else when that person makes a particular statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in March 1991, did the Presidency session take place which we have been mentioning here at which the proposal for the introduction of a state of emergency was rejected?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have discussed this topic already yesterday. My answer yesterday was that I remember that there has been a SFRY Presidency session in March 1991 where the proposal of Kadijevic to declare a state of emergency, I think it was, was rejected by the members, but I think I added yesterday that I didn't analyse the minutes or other reports of SFRY Presidency sessions, so I cannot go beyond the answer I gave yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. In the paragraph you have just read out, which is Kadijevic's statement addressing the public, does Mr. Kadijevic mention any other member of the SFRY Presidency in addition to the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, who, as he puts it, "prevented the making of decisions with a clear goal of breaking up Yugoslavia by hindering and breaking the army"? Did he mention anybody else?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this particular paragraph, Mr. Kadijevic or General Kadijevic speaks about the Supreme Commander we have, and then he also mentions federal Prime Minister. Now, I think I was also asked questions about this by Mr. Black during my examination, and the only thing I could conclude from my point of view as a military analyst was that the situation is very serious when the most senior military person in a country expresses such views about his political Supreme Commander, especially when he does that in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Theunens, that this was indeed a serious matter. However, when Mr. Kadijevic in his public statement accuses the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic, and the president of the Presidency, we shall not mention his name, of treason, both of the country and the army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you wish me to comment on this, I don't see the word treason in the paragraph. I only see -- I mean, one can conclude from reading the paragraph that General Kadijevic has very negative views on his political Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite -- I don't understand what is meant by, "Is that correct?" What do you want this witness to say, Mr. Milovancevic? Mr. Kadijevic said what he said. Is it for this witness to come and tell us whether it was correct or not correct to say what he said? Where are you going with that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The goal of my question aimed -- was the conclusion of the witness, who presented this particular conclusion after having quoted Mr. Kadijevic's statement and it's to be found on page 78 of the report. It's at the top of the page, right below the statement by Mr. Kadijevic, where the expert states, "This statement not only clarified the views of the SSNO on the objectives of the JNA in the conflict." The end of the sentence or rather the conclusion by Mr. Theunens is, "Kadijevic did not recognise their authority and attacked them in public."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He says nothing about correct or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you're saying, Mr. Milovancevic. You referred us to this paragraph because you're saying he said somewhere that it is correct or incorrect. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The essence of my question is the following, Your Honour: That the expert in this particular sentence states that the Kadijevic's statement expresses the views of the SSNO in relation to the objectives of the JNA. The expert quotes General Kadijevic, who stated that the tasks and the role of the JNA and the armed forces changed in the conflict that erupted, and explains the underlying reasons. My question aimed at the following: Such a public statement by General Kadijevic, is it the result of the fact that the president of the state and the Prime Minister disagreed with the changing of the role of the armed forces or is Mr. Kadijevic's statement in fact a reaction to the conduct displayed by the president of the state and Prime Minister Markovic, whom Mr. Kadijevic accuses of treason? The question was rather -- was a rather long one, but that was the drift of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is just the problem, Mr. Milovancevic. I still don't know what the question is after all this long statement. I'm just talking about asking the witness to state whether it is correct or incorrect for Kadijevic to make certain statements and I'm saying, where are we going with that question? That's the essence of my query. It has nothing to do with this long explanation that you've just given because I do not think it takes this case anywhere for this witness to say whether Kadijevic was correct or incorrect. He's only told us what Kadijevic said; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
