utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in all respect, expert witness Mr. Theunens ties up the lack of respect that Mr. Kadijevic shows vis-a-vis the Prime Minister and the president of the Presidency with the attempt at changing the role of the armed forces. This is the link that the expert makes in his report, because at the beginning he says that this statement serves to explain not only the objectives of the JNA but also that Kadijevic did not recognise the authority and publicly attacked the Prime Minister and head of state. My question to the expert was: This public display by General Kadijevic, did it have as its goal an attempt to change the role of the armed forces, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Put it that way. Don't ask him whether it is correct or not correct. Ask him just what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the attack and the lack of respect that you mention, which Mr. Kadijevic, as you put it, expressed vis-a-vis the president of the Presidency and the Prime Minister, did they have, as their goal, the change -- the changing of the constitutional role of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure whether I understand the question, but when we stick with this statement here, 65 ter number 1850, at the bottom of page 77 in my report, so in the English version, I quote the following paragraph from General Kadijevic's statement. "The army now wants nothing more but to restore control in the crisis areas, to protect the Serbian population from persecution and annihilation and to liberate the army personnel and members of their families. The condition for this is to defeat the Ustasha forces." This to me seems like Kadijevic expressing a mission for the armed forces, for the SFRY armed forces, and this mission is not included in the constitutional missions we addressed earlier today and also during my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Theunens, what the restoration of control in the crisis area, protection of the Serbian population from persecution and the liberation of the army personnel you've been mentioning, have to do with the personal relations between General Kadijevic, Prime Minister Markovic, and the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I ever suggested in my report that the nature of the relations between Kadijevic and the federal Prime Minister, Markovic, and the president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, had or were the causes of the change in the mission of the JNA. The reason why I read out this paragraph is the fact that it's included in the same public statement Kadijevic made on the 3rd of October 1991. So if anyone -- if anybody is making a link, well, from this document, it can only be Kadijevic, because in one paragraph in the beginning of the report, he criticises his Supreme Commander and then later on in a later paragraph in his statement from the 3rd of October, he describes his views on the role or what the JNA -- what the army should be doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard of the statement by President Mesic upon leaving the SFRY Presidency as having said, "I've accomplished my mission. Yugoslavia is no more." Do you know that Ante Markovic abandoned the Yugoslav government in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my report focuses on the SAO Krajina and RSK TO and SVK and relations between these organisations and Milan Martic. Analysing or studying developments within the SFRY executive -- federal executive council, of which Ante Markovic was chief, as Prime Minister, was not part or is not part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, your task as an expert was to analyse the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina and the RSK. You seem to be invoking this task of yours only when you find it inconvenient to answer a question that may gainsay what you state in your thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe this is an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got two more minutes, Mr. -- unless you're saying that the -- it's convenient for you. Is it a convenient time, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn and come back at half past 12. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we've mentioned the Geneva agreement on the 23rd of November 1991 signed by Mr. Kadijevic, Tudjman, Milosevic -- and Milosevic in the presence of Cyrus Vance. Did this agreement provide for an urgent cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if my recollection is correct, this agreement signed in Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991 provided for a cease-fire as well as included -- it included also modalities for the lifting of the blockades of barracks of the JNA that were still under blockade in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did this agreement say what was going to happen to the blocked barracks after the siege was lifted?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't recall the specific aspects of the agreement. I would have to see the agreement in order to be able to discuss those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. On page 80 of your report, you include a directive issued by the army general, Veljko Kadijevic, on the 10th of December 1991. You also testified about this directive. The title of this document is, "The directive on the use of the armed forces for the preparation and performance of combat operations in the forthcoming period." Is that correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, would you please read out paragraph 2 of this directive? It can be found on page 81 of your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I can add that this is 65 ter number 1277. So I read out the second paragraph. "In the foregoing period, the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia apart from the -- increasing their numbers and organisation have suffered heavy losses along the entire front line especially following the fall of Vukovar which has had a significant influence on the development of events at the political level. However, despite this, the opponent is striving to recover parts of its lost territory by constant combat activity. Therefore we must expect that in the forthcoming period by means of armed strikes, attacks, and actions. It will try to maintain the state of conflict with the intention of causing losses to our armed forces, improving its position on the front line, and influencing the political resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, above all via the institutions of the EC and the UN Security Council. This points to the conclusion that the war may continue for longer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In this directive, did Mr. Kadijevic speak about the final goals of the war?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. Under the heading, Roman II, which follows paragraph 3, at the beginning, Kadijevic says, and I will read it out, "Our armed forces are entering this a new period of exceptional significance for accomplishing the ultimate aims of the war, protection of the Serb population, a peaceful resolution of the Yugoslav crisis, and the creation of conditions in which Yugoslavia may be preserved for those people that wish to live in it." And the paragraph continues but I think that we mentioned the most relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. That's correct. That's precisely what I had in mind. Does General Kadijevic, after this, specify the tasks enumerating them in items 1 through 6? You bring that on page 82 and 83 of your report. Does General Kadijevic then give direct instructions to the armed forces as to what needs to be done in order to raise combat readiness in response to the anticipated moves of the enemy?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is correct that General Kadijevic gives a number of tasks. I think there are 12 -- 13 of them but I'm not sure whether they are entirely in response to what he perceives as the outlook or what he perceives as the probable Croatian course of action. It would be logical to link what Kadijevic sees as the Croatian intentions to the tasks he gives to the SFRY armed forces in order to act or pre-empt these Croatian intentions, to act against or pre-empt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Can you explain to us what your conclusion then means, your conclusion which follows immediately the quoted text of the directive, on page 83, where you state, I'm paraphrasing now, that such a directive was issued by Mr. Kadijevic at the time when the international community was making efforts aimed at finding a peaceful settlement or a resolution?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the text that follows in the top of page 83, so that follows the quotation from Kadijevic's directive is in my view not a conclusion but it's just an observation, and the only link -- if I wanted to establish a link, the only link I want to establish is that on the 10th of December, Kadijevic issues this directive, whereas on the 23rd of November 1991, a cease-fire agreement had been concluded. I don't think you will find additional conclusions from my side on whether there is a link between both and what this link then may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: By presenting such a comment, do you attribute to Mr. Kadijevic some war goals which would be beyond the UN peace efforts?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't understand the question. I mean the answer is no. But I didn't suggest any link between both things so it's difficult for me to attribute something then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can add, Kadijevic himself more or less states that the ultimate aims of the war or more or less accomplished. He doesn't say that in such strong terms in this directive but when we refer back to his book, it is quite obvious that by then, what he calls the second stage or the second phase of the operations in Croatia has been finalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that at the time when the Geneva agreement was signed, the phase of the war with the goals described by Mr. Kadijevic was already finalised? I didn't quite understand you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kadijevic in his book, when he talks about the second stage of the second phase, he doesn't mention the November 1991 cease-fire agreement. However, when we look at the developments of the military situation after the 23rd of November until the acceptance of the Vance Plan, with the exception of the Dubrovnik area, the most significant operations -- JNA operations had been concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that the JNA's obligation stemming from the Vance Plan to withdraw its troops from the territory of Croatia is a significant JNA operation? Is that what you believe?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, any withdrawal operation that concerns forces of the size the JNA still had in Croatia before the acceptance of the Vance Plan is indeed a significant operation, no matter what significance you give to the word "significant" or which meaning you give to the word "significant".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that the cease-fire agreement from Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991 was the 13th cease-fire agreement since the eruption of the conflict in August of 1991? Or perhaps even the 14th, chronologically. I'm trying to say that there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were indeed many cease-fire agreements prior to the one that was signed in Geneva on the 23rd of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that many of such cease-fire agreements were signed precisely at the insistence of the international community, the European Community, and the United States?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, even though I didn't analyse the cease-fire agreements and the motives for them and the organisations or people who brokered them, it is indeed obvious that the international community tried to achieve a peaceful solution for the conflict in Yugoslavia and, of course, in order to create the conditions to achieve such a peaceful solution, a cease-fire agreement is one of the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell us that based on the book of General Kadijevic, the purpose of the second phase of the armed conflict was to defeat the Croatian armed forces? Wasn't that one of the goals?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on what Kadijevic writes in -- on page 00362709 in the English translation of his book, the task of the JNA during the second phase was to, and I quote, "Protect the Serb population in Croatia in such a way that all regions with a majority Serb population would be completely freed from the presence of the Croatian army and the Croatian authorities." Then he adds, "To pull the JNA out of Croatia by first ensuring that the above task was completed." And third aspect, "To carry out the continued country-wide transformation of the JNA into the army of the future Yugoslavia, focusing on its internal, national, and organisational structure and its territorial location." And, of course, when he then details, and that's in the following pages in his book, more specifically 00362710, Kadijevic specifies the missions during the two stages he distinguishes in what he calls the second phase of the conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your experience as a military expert and as a military person, 13 interruptions of a mission can represent an obstacle for attaining a military goal.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, I can give a general answer but it all depends on the mission and the kind of interruption. It's obvious that if you try to achieve something, whatever you do, whether it's a military goal or you pursue a political goal or another goal, if you're interrupted, then it hinders you in achieving that goal, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. We said that on the 23rd of November 1991, in Geneva, the foundation was created for the UN peace operation. That was the preparation for the Vance Plan. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the UN Secretary-General's report submitted to the Security Council, number S-23280, dated the 11th of December 1991? In this report, the Secretary-General warns the Security Council of the dangers that the UN peace mission could encounter in the form of premature recognition of seceding republics?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours I may have seen this specific report of the UN Secretary-General to the Security Council before coming to the ICTY but I don't recall seeing it while working at the ICTY. I am familiar with the reports from February 1992 as well as the one I think from 28th of September 1992 which is quoted in my report and also one from November 1992 which is also mentioned in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you followed these reports in relation to your work, may I remind you that on the 11th of December 1991, the UN Secretary-General informs the Security Council of the information he received from Cyrus Vance, the UN special envoy, about the fact that the premature recognition of republics which want to secede would represent a disaster for the region?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so, I assume it's correct, but it would be helpful for me to see the report and to also see in which context Mr. Vance makes these comments and look at the other parts of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We have an e-court system here. Defence has a minor technical problem and we will attempt to resolve it later on and show you this document, which is report S-23280 of the UN Secretary-General dated the 11th of December 1991. In that report, Mr. Theunens, the Secretary-General not only warns the Security Council of the dangers associated with premature recognition but also writes a letter to the presiding chairman of the European council, Mr. van den Broek, warning him of this danger and asking him not to recognise any of the republics prior to finding an overall solution to the crisis. Are you familiar with this text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt, Mr. Milovancevic? Is there any way the officials can help with the technical problem you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have in front of me the report. However, it's been underlined, and I don't think it is suitable to show it to the witness in this form. Therefore I propose that we do it later. I have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's not a technical problem. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Vatican recognised the independence of Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know when the Vatican recognised the independence of Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the Vatican recognised Croatia or rather Slovenia as an independent country on the 13th of January 1992, whereas Germany and some other European countries did that on the 15th of January 1992, would you say that was reasonable?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that that is correct, that these are the dates when certain countries, including Germany, recognised Slovenia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when we discussed the acceptance of the Vance Plan or rather the UN Security Council resolution 743 from February 1992, did we conclude that the peace operation in Yugoslavia was created in February of 1992 pursuant to a Security Council resolution?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the UN peace operation? Because there were other peace efforts ongoing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Yes. I mean the UN peace operation.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could phrase it like that. I mean, if you take UN Security Council resolution 743 as the basis, then it would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that one of the goals and objectives for deployment of the peace forces throughout Yugoslavia pursuant to that resolution was to create conditions for peace in order to achieve an overall settlement of the Yugoslav crisis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. But now that I see the transcript, the deployment of peace forces was mainly in Croatia. The UNPROFOR headquarters initially was located in Sarajevo, but I'm not aware of any significant deployment of UN peace forces in -- at that stage in other republics of the former Yugoslavia, and I'm mainly thinking of Slovenia or Serbia-Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the Vance Plan provide for the UN peace operation in Yugoslavia and does it specify all of the goals that are to be achieved in the course of that operation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, the Vance Plan as I mentioned during my examination consists of three phases and the things that had to be achieved during these three phases could be considered the goals of the Vance Plan as well as the goals that were to be pursued at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the decision to send the UN peace mission to Yugoslavia and to establish UNPROFOR was to find a peaceful settlement of the crisis and of the conflict without prejudging its outcome? Do you remember that something to that effect was stated in the text?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, the Vance Plan mentions that more specifically in relation to the UNPAs, that the arrangements are of an interim nature and that they are intended to create conditions of peace and security in order to allow negotiations for political solution, and also that this deployment does not prejudge the outcome of these negotiations for a comprehensive settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since the Vance Plan emphasises that it does not wish to prejudge the political negotiations for the comprehensive settlement of the crisis does not the premature recognition of Croatia and Slovenia by some countries prejudge the outcome of the negotiations, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a political question, but I can mention that I can add that the resolutions, UN -- United Nations Security Council resolutions that were adopted in 1992 and that deal specifically with the situation in Croatia emphasise the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Theunens. However, the UN peace operation was intended for Yugoslavia. All at once, there is discussion of an independent Croatia. Does not this -- does this not constitute a prejudging of the situation even by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that I'm the appropriate person to answer that question. I can give a personal comment on it but I wonder to what extent I'm qualified to do so. All I can say is that the -- as I mentioned already, that the resolution that concern the deployment of UNPROFOR and subsequent resolution that -- resolutions that deal with the extension of the mandate of UNPROFOR mention the territorial integrity of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. We shall briefly go back to page 83 of your report, where, following the quotation of parts of the directive by Mr. Kadijevic and the order by General Adzic, under paragraph F on page 83, you say, "The instructions from what remained of the SFRY Presidency, Kadijevic's analysis and Adzic's order, indicate that the JNA moved towards ceasing to be the SFRY army and instead gradually developed into a mainly Serb force serving Serbian goals." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add, Your Honours, that this -- in this subparagraph F, it says that at least in Croatia, the JNA moved towards ceasing to be the SFRY army and instead gradually developed into a mainly Serb force. I think that's a significant aspect of the conclusion I draw here because I only look at the mission and the way how the JNA is implementing that in Croatia, not in the other parts of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Theunens. That's precisely my question. Can you tell us which were these Serb goals that the JNA served in Croatia and that you mention here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we have -- I've discussed them but again, let's go back to the book of Kadijevic. Kadijevic and more specifically we don't have to go to each phase in detail but when we go to the second phase, he talks about, and I'm reading now from page 73, subparagraph B between brackets, "The task of the JNA was to protect the Serb people in Croatia in such a way that all regions with a majority Serb population would be completely freed from the presence of the Croatian army and the Croatian authorities." It clearly mentions Serb population. It doesn't mention what is to happen with the non-Serbs because, again, and that's maybe outside of the scope of my report but when the Kadijevic says that regions with a majority Serb population would be completely present -- completely freed from the presence of the Croatian army and the Croatian authorities, now, the question that then can be raised is what is to happen with non-Serbs who live in these areas and who want to stay in an area that is controlled by the Croatian authorities? Kadijevic doesn't address that. Now, we can continue when we look at the next pages, and when Kadijevic specifies the missions during the second phase, he talks about the first stage, which I discuss on page 74 in my report, English version, subparagraph D, first stage, "the operations focused primarily on tactically important counterattacks until Croatian aggression came fully to fore, while at the same time intensively organising and preparing Serb in Croatia." He specifies that further. I'm not going to read that out in detail. It can be found in my report. When coming then to the second stage of the second phase, which is mentioned -- which is explained - excuse me - on page 76 of the English version of my report, Kadijevic mentions "the main tasks, of the modified plan," I can only mention -- I can mention the two of them. First one, "in close coordination with the Serb insurgents, all subregions in Croatia except for a part in Western Slavonia were liberated and he states that this corresponds with approximately one third of the territory of the Republic of Croatia," and then second task, "the future army of the Serbian Krajina was actually built up in the course of fighting and equipped by the JNA with corresponding arms and materials." I think that Kadijevic is much better placed than me to identify these goals, these Serbian goals, that are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Your answer was rather long, but failed to give an answer to my question. I did not ask you about what General Kadijevic had to say about the goals but, rather, about your conclusion on page 93 that -- or rather, 83, that the JNA's role changed in the direction of merely serving the Serb goals. My question to you was: Which were these Serb goals?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you have the most senior person in a country identify in great detail goals the armed forces of that country had to pursue, who am I to have doubts about these goals? I can only repeat what Kadijevic said. Why should I try to conclude something else? I think Kadijevic is very clear, as well as the orders and statements that Kadijevic and Adzic issued during the latter half of 1991. There is no reason for me to draw additional conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this is your military expert report. In addition to General Kadijevic's book, you cited a number of documents on the basis of an analysis of all these documents, you state here that the JNA served the Serb goals whereas General Kadijevic and Adzic speak of the protection of the Serb population. Can you remember see the difference there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Kadijevic and Adzic indeed mention the protection of the Serb population but Kadijevic also, as I just read out, mentions the liberation of Serb regions. Now, Serb regions as such were not defined in Croatia, as far as my research allows me to conclude. There were of course areas with a significant Serb presence, Serb majority and already for centuries. There is no doubt about that. But in these areas there were also non-Serbs. Now, when you read Kadijevic's book, actually the goal there, he understands or he sees liberating these areas as removing Croatian military and Croatian authority. Now, I think the goal there is pretty obvious. The organising of the future army of the Serbian Krajina I think that is also quite clear as a goal. So I don't -- I really don't know what I can add to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not insist on this matter any further, Your Honour, but I believe that the witness did not answer my question as to what the Serb goals were. He spoke of the JNA's withdrawal of the forces, a blockade of the barracks, the creation of the forces of the RSK, all these are goals that General Kadijevic mentions, who, I should say in passing, was born to one of whose parents were Croat. I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I meant in relation to this topic, Your Honour. I apologise. I only wish to say that I will not pursue the matter of the Serbian goals any longer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just informed that we do have the UN report which is number 65 ter number 813 on e-court. This is the report dated 11 December 1991. When I said that we had some technical difficulties, I meant the Defence had technical difficulties rather than that we were not offered enough assistance by court officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. You are now better understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I don't have any objection to looking at this document but it does raise a procedural point which I think should be addressed now. I have not -- I was not aware that this document was going to be used. It's on our 65 ter list. I don't have any problem with it being used but ordinarily the practice at this Tribunal is at the beginning of cross-examination, we are provided with a documents that the Defence intends to use during cross-examination. They can be released to e-court, in fact is I believe how the process was explained to me. That was not done in this case. It's not a problem with there document but I can imagine at sometimes documents that come up a that I haven't seen and I might have to ask for a delay in order to prepare. I can see no reason beyond simple surprise why these kind of documents couldn't be released or identified to me at the beginning of cross-examination rather than piecemeal as we go through the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the practice indicated by my learned colleague from the OTP may prevail before some of the Trial Chambers but I believe that such a burden placed on the Defence would prejudice its cross-examination, on the one side. Only after the Prosecutor completes his examination-in-chief can the Defence decide which documents it will use during cross-examination. I don't think that such obligations placed on the Defence can be realised. Besides, this is an exhibit from the Prosecution's 65 ter list. We did experience some technical difficulties. However, since the witness himself stated that it would be good for him to see the document, the Defence did it -- its utmost to make sure that the document was presented both to the witness and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, one thing just to clarify, I'm certainly not suggesting that if during the course of direct examination or particularly during the course of cross-examination it becomes apparent that Defence counsel needs to refer to some other document that was not on his list, they would certainly be free to do that. I'm not suggesting that their hands be tied by any list that they provide to us. But if this was -- again I'm not objecting to this particular document but all such documents as could reasonably be identified at the beginning of cross-examination should be provided to us. We, of course, provide a list of documents to the Defence before we start our direct examination, and while I'm not suggesting either that they have to do that in advance, as we do, certainly at the beginning of cross seems like the reasonable time, Your Honour. That's my request, going into the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, do you have any Rule of the Tribunal on which you rely for that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I'm aware, this does not appear in the Rules of Evidence and Procedure. I'm relying on my experience in the Limaj trial which was included last year and also in the Brdjanin trial which concluded a couple of years ago. I'm not aware of any case that it was done differently although certainly that may have happened on cases in which I did not participate. I can try to collect jurisprudence, Your Honour, but I don't think there will be any written decisions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, do you have any other documents that you intend using during the cross-examination of this witness that you have not shown to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this time the Defence does not have a single document before it which does not come from the 65 ter list. This issue has been raised just now. I would not wish to give you an incomplete answer. However, based on the experience so far in cross-examination, we have no such other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No such what documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have, for the time being, any plans to introduce or to tender documents that are not contained on the OTP 65 ter list. Therefore, all these are documents contained in the Prosecutor's list. We have not had the obligation to deliver such a list in advance because there was no such decision taken by the Trial Chamber, and there was no such proposal on the part of the Prosecution. If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to address you on another matter. In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we finalise this matter first before you address me on another matter? My question to you had been: Do you have any other documents, irrespective of where they come from, whether they come from the 65 ter list or from anywhere else, do you have any other documents that you intend tendering into evidence during your cross-examination of this particular witness? If you have them, say yes. If you don't have them, say no. Apart from the one that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you in a position to indicate to the Prosecution what those documents are?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber should decide that we are duty bound to do so, then we will comply. I wanted to refer you to the cases before the Tribunal, Naletilic, Martinovic, Halilovic case, then the Vukovar case, Blagojevic/Jokic case. In none of these cases was there an obligation in place for the Defence to provide the Prosecution with a list of documents in advance of their examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well, then. Mr. Black has no objection to your tendering this document that you're about to tender. You are referring to cases that you say there was no such obligation. He has referred to cases where he says that such lists were tendered. However, Mr. Black does also say that there is no Rule of the Tribunal that forces you to do so. So I will make no ruling on the issue on this matter, unless somebody makes -- submits a motion for a ruling. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to briefly point out that the Defence will do its utmost to proceed correctly in this case, and to avoid creating any difficulties for the OTP or informing them of some matters on short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that undertaking, Mr. Milovancevic. The Court appreciates that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You wanted to go to another matter. Can you go to that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the document I requested on the monitor, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking the legal -- the Court officials to help, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I requested that the Registry show us the 65 ter Exhibit 813, place on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the entire first page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, before you is the document by the Security Council, S-23280, dated 11 December 1991. In the paragraphs 1, 3, and 4, on page 1, do you see that the Security Council speaks of a peace operation in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, it's mentioned at the end of paragraph 4. It talks about the possible establishment of United Nations peacekeeping operations in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be shown paragraph 25? That's on page 8 of the report, for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can you please read out paragraph 25?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 25, "A soundly based and effective cease-fire would further open the way for constructive negotiations between the representatives of the republics. In this respect, the conference on Yugoslavia under the Chairmanship of Lord Carrington enjoys the full support of the Security Council as reflected in resolution 713 of 1991. The conference has been adjourned since 5 November, although Lord Carrington held an informal stock taking session with the presidents of Yugoslavia's six republics on 9 December. The conference, it will be recalled, is guided by a number of considerations, including those set forth in the declaration issued by the 12 member states of the European Community at Rome on 8 November 1991," then between brackets S/23203, "that declaration stated inter alia that, 'The prospect of recognition of the independence of those republics wishing it can only be envisaged in the framework of an overall settlement.'" End of quotation. "The conference has also, with the agreement of its participants, ruled out any changes in external or internal borders by means of force. I believe that any selective uncoordinated departure from those principles could hold very serious dangers not only for the republics of Yugoslavia but for all of her peoples and indeed for the maintenance of peace and security in" -- and I--

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. In addition to the report, there is annex 4, in view of the fact that at the end of paragraph 25, UN Secretary-General said that on the 10th of December 1991, he had -- he sent a letter to the presiding chairman of the European community, Mr. van den Broek.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather of the European council. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please be shown annex 4 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours? If you allow me, when I was asked earlier questions about the risks, recognition or premature recognition would entail, I asked to see the report. And when we see now the paragraph 24, it mentions not only the risks of premature recognition as a potential factor for -- cause for trouble in the future but also the changes into internal or external borders. So I think we need to be complete when we address these issues. In this paragraph 24, the Secretary-General talks about two principles that need to be respected, the principle of non-premature recognition and the principle of inchangeability of the borders, internal and external.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can you tell us, did the Republic of Croatia change the state borders of Yugoslavia by using armed force?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would -- I mean, again this is a question which is outside my qualifications. I can only refer to the report we have been looking at now that says in paragraph 24 that one of the two principles that need to be respected is the principle of the inviolability of internal and external borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, would you please read out the last sentence of paragraph 25? The last sentence of paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I addressed a letter to the current president of the council of ministers of the European Community, foreign minister van den Broek of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, the text of which is reproduced as annex 4 to the present report."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that despite these warnings, there was a de facto recognition of Slovenia and Croatia in January of 1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I have the required background to be able to make an authoritative statement on the fact whether it was a de facto or any other recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this document into evidence, Your Honours, as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document may be -- admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 104, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we will now turn to another section of your expert report. This is the topic known as the TO of the SAO Krajina. It starts on page 84 of your expert report. In paragraph 1, which is an introduction, you say that already prior to the eruption of hostilities in Croatia, the police and TO of the Republic of Croatia were divided into Croatian and Serb structures. Can you tell us who implemented this division or split?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be a translation issue but I didn't phrase the -- that paragraph exactly as it has been put here. What I wrote, and I will read it out, is that "already prior to the eruption of hostilities in Croatia, the police and TO of the Republic of Croatia gradually split into Croatian and local Serb structures." So I want to emphasise it was a gradual process. Based on the documents I reviewed, there are several situations in, on one hand, you can see that on the local level, in particular in areas with a Serb majority or a significant minority, local Serbs create their own structure. But I've also seen that the documents -- the issue I'm discussing now, these documents are not included in the report, that in some cases the Croats say that they don't want to be part of the TO any more or don't want to be part of the police any more and they create their own structures. There are also examples where from the Knin level, from the SAO Krajina level, instructions are given to create local Serb TO forces in a number of areas with a significant Serb minority or a Serb majority and the latter is also happening with assistance of the JNA or as we have seen in -- as is visible in a number of examples the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia. And this is a process that takes place more or less between January and December 1991 but becomes more intensified after summer 1991. And that's what I've attempted to describe in this section from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You speak about gradual division of the police and Territorial Defence into Serbian and Croatian component. Did these two processes evolve simultaneously or did one start before the other? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise, I didn't look at the process that resulted in the Croatian -- of local Serb police forces so I can't really say whether the TO was created prior to the police or the police prior to the TO. From a document we discussed during examination, that spoke about the situation in Benkovac, and that was 65 ter number 1851, there it appears, at least in the Benkovac area that the local Serb police started to be organised at an earlier stage than the local Serb TO, and as a result was better equipped and better organised. And 1851 is mentioned on the top of page 86.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Continuing this sentence in paragraph 1, you say that the areas where local Serbs had a majority or a significant minority were the areas where they took over existing structures, and that they remained loyal to what remained of the SFRY and Serbia. Is that true, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe again it's a translation issue but the phrase that was put was in areas where the Serbs had a majority or significant minority they took over existing structures. At least in my understanding this sentence does not suggest that in all areas where local Serbs had a majority or significant minority they took over existing structures or created their own TOs. Otherwise, Mr. Milovancevic is correct in what he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this process commenced in 1991, roughly in January 1991. What is this concept of what remained of Yugoslavia that you are talking about then, when Slovenia and Croatia did not secede until much later, end of June 1991?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the subtitle "historical background" on page 84, it has the heading, A, which is under the heading 4, SAO Krajina TO, it says January to December 1991. So the text that follows below is, of course, a reflection or applies to the entire time period between January and December 1991. So it also includes the latter half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. What do you say about the conduct of non-Serbs in that period of time, which is the next sentence after the one talking about Serbs taking over existing structures? What can you tell us about the conduct of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on the documents I looked at, the documents I looked at to try to understand and then describe the creation of a local Serb SAO Krajina TO, it appeared that non-Serbs in some areas, they left, or they were encouraged to leave, or they didn't recognise the SFRY any more and they ceased their cooperation with the JNA. It's hard for me now to come up with specific documents on specific situations that I related to specific areas but when you look at these various documents and they will follow when -- also on page 85 I discuss the evolution, these things I have mentioned on the actions undertaken by the non-Serbs are visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Based on what you wrote in the first paragraph that we just quoted, Mr. Theunens, could we say that in that period of time, gradually, police and Territorial Defence in Croatia split into the Croatian and Serb component and that the Serb component remained loyal to the SFRY, whereas the Croatian component refused to comply?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that that reflects what this paragraph says. What I say in this paragraph goes beyond the fact that, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I apologise for interrupting you. I didn't say that this is what you wrote in your paragraph. My question was could we say, based on everything you testified about, that the situation was as I have described it? You can certainly answer on the basis of the sources that you are familiar with. So I'm not asking you about the meaning of the text that you wrote here. I'm simply asking you whether such a conclusion can be drawn.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish that my reply reflects my report, which is then based on sources I reviewed. I don't think I put it the way as Mr. Milovancevic puts it. I don't think I wrote it that way in my report, because, as we know, Territorial Defence was a republican organisation and they were answerable for a number of issues, combat readiness, training, and related issues, to the republican authorities. It is correct that they were subordinated to the SFRY Supreme Command. Now, the Territorial Defence in the Republic of Croatia was a republican structure which covered the entire territory of the Republic of Croatia and we see that, as I tried to describe, a gradual split occurs whereby local Serb structures are set up in areas with a significant Serb presence. Now, these local Serb structures, they see that the goals they are pursuing are also being pursued by the JNA, so it's quite logical that these local Serb structures remained loyal to the SFRY and that Croatian structures preferred to be loyal to the government of the Republic of Croatia. So I don't think it is correct to state, as Mr. Milovancevic stated, that the Croatian structures were not complying with SFRY structures -- with SFRY leadership any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I don't mean to interrupt you. I'll ask that we stop at quarter to because of other engagements that the Chamber has to do, to attend to. We are left with about half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I was about to propose that we adjourn for the day. We will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is very grateful to you for that. The matter then stands postponed to the 3rd of February at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of February 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
